title: Jagadisha Pandita
html:
A Branch of Two Trees

Sri Jagadisha Pandita is one of those companions of Sri Chaitanya whom the Lord blessed with His mercy already in His childhood pastimes. Krishnadasa Kaviraja, counting the branches of Chaitanya's tree, speaks of him together with Hiranya:

“Jagadisha Pandita and Hiranya Mahashaya received the compassionate Lord's mercy when He was still a child.” (CC, Adi 10.70)

“In these two houses, on the day of Ekadashi, the Lord begged for the food offered to Vishnu and ate it Himself.” (CC, Adi 10.71)

Yet the same Kaviraja names him also among the branches of Nityananda's tree:

“Sri Jagadisha Pandita purifies the whole world; like a heavy monsoon rain, he pours down the nectar of love for Krishna.” (CC, Adi 11.30)

He is therefore counted a branch of both Sri Chaitanya and Nityananda. Vrindavana Dasa Thakura, listing the companions of Nityananda, says of him:

“Jagadisha Pandita is the supreme abode of radiant holiness; Nityananda with His companions was his wealth and his life.” (CB, Antya 5.736)

The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” calls him Jagadisha and Sri Jagadisha Pandita, the “Charitamrita” Jagadisha Pandita; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in his “Anubhashya” calls him both Jagadisha Bhatta and Jagadisha Pandita Goswami, and the biographies call him Sri Jagadisha Pandita Prabhu.1

Chandrahasa

Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes is revealed by Kavi Karnapura:

“Chandrahasa, the dancer of Vraja, a knower of rasa, is the lover of dance Sri Jagadisha Pandita.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 143)

In Vraja he is Chandrahasa, a dancer who knows the taste of rasa; and now too, in Gaura's pastimes, Jagadisha loves to dance in the Lord's kirtana. As “the dancer” the vandanas — songs in glorification of the Vaishnavas — also remember him.

Elsewhere in the same list Karnapura speaks of him and of Hiranya:

“Other wives of the sacrificial priests are Sri Jagadisha and Hiranyaka, whose food the Lord asked for and ate on Ekadashi.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 192)

The wives of the brahmana priests engaged in sacrifice (yajna-patni) fed Krishna in His pastimes; now they appeared as Jagadisha and Hiranya to nourish the pastimes of Gaura — and again the Lord asked them for food. The biographies cite the two verses in one order — first 192, then 143 — as Srila Bhaktisiddhanta does in the “Anubhashya.”2

From Gauhati to the Ganga

Jagadisha appeared in the east of India, in Gauhati — ancient Prag-jyotishapura, now in Assam. He was the son of Kamalaksha Bhatta; according to the “Anubhashya,” he came of the line of Bhatta-narayana.3 His father and mother were householders and great devotees of Vishnu.

When his parents left this world, Jagadisha, with his wife Dukhini and his brother, left his native land and came to the Ganga, to Sri Mayapur. There he built a house next to the house of Jagannatha Mishra and settled in it. Which brother came with him the sources tell differently: according to some, Hiranya Pandita; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya,” retelling the tradition of the shripat at Yashada, names the brother Mahesha — Jagadisha settled by the Ganga to live in the company of Vaishnavas. But whether this Mahesha is Mahesha Pandita, one of the twelve gopalas, the authoritative books, he remarks elsewhere in the same “Anubhashya,” do not say, “and therefore it is doubtful.”4

A close, heartfelt friendship bound Jagadisha to Jagannatha Mishra. Vrindavana Dasa writes of him and Hiranya:

“The Panditas Jagadisha and Hiranya were great Vaishnavas, one in life with Jagannatha Mishra.” (CB, Adi 6.26)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta adds in his “Gaudiya-bhashya” on these verses that Mishra cherished these two brahmanas dearly: they were bound to him by the ties of an unbreakable friendship.

Jagadisha's wife was named Dukhini; she is also called Dukhini-mata. He and Dukhini loved Nimai just as Jagannatha Mishra and Shachi loved Him — with parental love, vatsalya. According to one of the biographies, Dukhini was like a mother to Nimai and at times even nursed Him at her breast. Such fortune falls only to the Lord's eternal associates: to treat God Himself as one's own child is possible only for those whom He Himself has called into this rasa.

Jagadisha showed the pastime of a householder. His son was Ramabhadra Goswami; according to the “Anubhashya,” his only son.

Jagadisha was born before the Lord, and not by chance. Vrindavana Dasa speaks of the eternal associates who by the Lord's will were born before Him and until the time came lived hidden in Nadia:

“By the order of Lord Chaitanya many of His eternal associates — Sri Chandrashekhara, Jagadisha, Gopinatha Acharya, Shriman Pandita, Murari Gupta, Sri Garuda Pandita and Gangadasa Pandita — were born before His coming and lived hidden in Nadia.” (CB, Adi 2.98–99)

The biographies quote the same verses in their chapters on Chandrashekhara and Gangadasa, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in his comment on them, lists the places in scripture where Jagadisha's name appears, from the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” to the “Charitamrita.”5

Ekadashi

How dear Jagadisha was to Him, the Lord showed while still an infant, in a childhood pastime.

Vrindavana Dasa, listing the pastimes of the Adi-khanda, names this one at once:

“In the Adi-khanda the Lord eats the grain prepared in the house of Jagadisha and Hiranya on the day of Ekadashi.” (CB, Adi 1.100)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in his “Gaudiya-bhashya”: the day of the Lord's appearance, Ekadashi and certain Dvadashis are called “Sri Hari-vasara,” the days of Hari; on these days the servants of Hari set aside their worldly affairs and serve Him by fasting. But Sri Vishvambhara is the Supreme Lord Himself, and so He did not fast as a devotee would, but accepted the dishes offered to Him. The rule of fasting applies to people, not to the Lord, who Himself lays down the rules: Sri Hari, the protector of His devotees, accepts the offering of His servants even on Hari-vasara. So Gaura-Narayana too wished to taste the dishes from the house of Jagadisha and Hiranya. Fasting is the service of the servants; this time the Lord did not show the pastime of the fast obligatory for them, but showed another pastime — accepting the offering prepared for Himself.

Mahaprabhu is the father of sankirtana, and already as an infant He made everyone chant the holy name. When He cried, Shachi and the neighbouring women would clap and chant Hari's names — and He would grow quiet:

“There was, however, one sure remedy: as soon as kirtana began, the Lord stopped crying. Whenever someone began to clap and sing the names of Hari, the Lord became quiet and docile. To keep the child content, everyone sang the holy names of God constantly, and the house of Jagannatha Mishra was like Sri Vaikuntha.” (CB, Adi 6.13–15)

But one day, on Ekadashi, Nimai would not be calmed, however much everyone sang. His anxious elders lovingly asked what He wanted, promising to bring Him anything at all. And He answered:

“The Lord replied: ‘If you want to save My life, go at once to the house of two brahmanas. Jagadisha and Hiranya are great devotees, and what I desire is with them. Today, on Ekadashi, they are both fasting, but they have prepared an offering for Lord Vishnu. When I eat it, I will stop crying and go out to play.’” (CB, Adi 6.20–23)

Hearing this, Shachi began to lament:

“‘What you ask for is permitted neither by people nor by the Vedas.’” (CB, Adi 6.24)

But the people around laughed and promised the child to bring Him prasada.

When Jagadisha and Hiranya learned of Nimai's wish, they saw in it neither a child's whim nor a breach of the fast. Vrindavana Dasa relates:

“Learning of the child's wish, these brahmanas were filled with joy. The brahmanas exclaimed: ‘What a wonderful request! We have never heard of so wise a child. How did He know that today is Ekadashi? How does He know that we have prepared many different dishes for the Lord? Now we understand why this child is so beautiful: surely Gopala-Krishna Himself is acting in His body.’” (CB, Adi 6.27–30)

“Then these brahmanas, with great joy, brought all the dishes. They said: ‘Child, taste these delicacies. Today our desire to render service to Krishna has been fulfilled.’” (CB, Adi 6.32–33)

Jagadisha, the Lord's eternal associate, recognized in Mishra's son Gopala, the son of Nanda, who wished to taste his offering in the form of Nimai, and together with Hiranya gave Him everything without hesitation. This is no breach of Ekadashi: the brahmanas gave the Lord His own bhoga, and in this the purpose of all their service to Krishna was fulfilled.6

Having received the offering from His devotees, Nimai's tears ceased and He ate with great joy, tasting a little of each dish, while all around chanted Hari's names, and He ate and danced (CB, Adi 6.37–39).

One of the biographies retells this pastime in its own way: Shachi struck her forehead in amazement, the women promised to fulfil the child's wish if He would stop crying, and Jagadisha and Hiranya, who had known before that Hari Himself had been born as Mishra's son, fed Him to His fill and said in jest that He had eaten Krishna's share. While Nimai ate, this biography says, there appeared to them the form of the infant Krishna — the colour of a fresh rain cloud, radiant, with a peacock feather — and in ecstasy they began to sing “Hari! Hari!” It also says that the little Lord came to their house Himself, and adds to His words: the devotees fast, but Vishnu is not bound by the fast and eats what He likes.7

Krishnadasa Kaviraja recalls this pastime in his account of the Lord's childhood:

“On the day of Ekadashi, pretending to be ill, He ate the food offered to Vishnu in the house of Jagadisha and Hiranya.” (CC, Adi 14.39)

And Vrindavana Dasa, much later, when Jagadisha and Hiranya set out for Nilachala, recalls again that in childhood the Lord had eaten the grain they offered to Krishna in their home on Ekadashi (CB, Antya 8.29). The Ekadashi story is told in the sixth chapter of the Adi-khanda of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata.”8

The biographies draw a lesson from this pastime: the Lord Himself snatches and eats what belongs to His devotee, but will not even glance at the gifts of one without devotion. Vrindavana Dasa says the same elsewhere:

“Thus the Lord enjoys the gifts of His devotees and pays no attention to millions of offerings from those devoid of devotion.” (CB, Madhya 9.185)

Nimai's request on Ekadashi is no breach of the fast but a pastime of God Himself: the servants keep the fast, and the Lord accepts what they have prepared for Him, and so shows how dear they are to Him.

The house of Jagadisha and Hiranya in Navadvipa where this took place is shown to pilgrims on the circuit of the dhama (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 12.1114, 12.2186). According to Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura's “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya,” it stood about a krosha to the south-east of Mishra's house — no child could have known what was being cooked there; according to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's “Gaudiya-bhashya,” the two brahmanas lived in Godrumadvipa, not far from Jagannatha Mishra's house.

In the Kirtanas of Navadvipa

When the Lord began sankirtana, Jagadisha was among the parshadas with whom He sang and danced every night in the house of Shrivasa, and sometimes at Chandrashekhara's, only with His associates. Vrindavana Dasa names him in the list of those present at these kirtanas (CB, Madhya 8.115).

The Lord was conquered by Jagadisha's pure devotion, and in the same way Nityananda, non-different from the Lord, was conquered by his love: He regarded Jagadisha as His own and loved him dearly.

After the deliverance of Jagai and Madhai, Jagadisha was among the devotees who sported with the Lord in the waters of the Ganga (CB, Madhya 13.336–339); on the day the Kazi was subdued, among those who went with the Lord in the night procession of kirtana through the town (CB, Madhya 23.150).9 And when in Shridhara's house the Lord drank water from his iron pot, Jagadisha wept with joy together with the others:

“Jagadisha, Gopinatha, Nandana Acharya, Shuklambara, Garuda and many other devotees shed tears.” (CB, Madhya 23.452)

The “Bhakti-ratnakara” and the vandanas glorify him among the Lord's associates. Narahari Chakravarti names him among those who sang with the Lord in Shrivasa's courtyard (BR 12.1888), and in the songs quoted in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” Jagadisha, “skilled in singing,” sings the song of the abhisheka when the Lord is bathed in Shrivasa's house, and with Damodara sings in the kirtana on the bank of the Ganga (BR 12.2702, 12.3150). His name stands also in the lists of the “Narottama-vilasa.”

Jagannatha from Purushottama

By the Lord's order Jagadisha went to Nilachala to spread krishna-bhakti and the religion of the age — the sankirtana of the names of Hari. When this was is not known for certain.10 Seeing in Purushottama Lord Jagannatha — the same Supreme Truth as Krishna, the son of Nanda, and Gaurasundara, the son of Jagannatha Mishra — Jagadisha was filled with prema, and on the way back he was overcome by longing in separation from Jagannatha, and wept.

Many see Jagannatha in Puri, but few, on leaving, long for Him in separation. One of the biographies observes: such longing is a sign of Jagannatha's mercy, and without it His mercy has not truly been received.

Seeing Jagadisha's tears, Jagannatha, full of mercy, came to him in a dream and bade him take His Deity and serve Him. Then too He ordered the king of Orissa of that day to give Jagadisha that form of His which, at the Nava-kalevara, the renewal of Jagannatha's body, had been “buried” (samadhistha-vigraha); according to one of the biographies, He appeared to the king, too, in a dream. This is not a form whose service had ended: it is Jagannatha Himself, who wished to accept Jagadisha's service. And the king counted it his good fortune to have met such a devotee, and held it a great honour to give him the Deity.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that Jagadisha prayed to Jagannathadeva and in answer was allowed to take the Deity away; one of the biographies, citing him, writes that Jagadisha, having asked Jagannatha's permission, took His Sri-murti to Yashada and installed Him there.

Jagadisha asked how so heavy a Deity could be carried. Jagannatha replied that He would grow as light as shola pith (according to another biography — as cork); Jagadisha should wrap Him in fresh cloth and bear Him on a pole over his shoulder, and lower Him to the ground at the place where he chose to install Him. One of the biographies adds: the place where He touched the earth would be Jagadisha's home for ever.

With the help of the brahmanas who accompanied him (according to one of the biographies, two, who carried the Deity in turns), Jagadisha brought Jagannatha to Yashada on the Ganga, within Chakdaha, in present-day West Bengal. There he handed Him to a brahmana servant to hold on his shoulder while he himself bathed in the Ganga and offered tarpana. Then Jagannatha suddenly became very heavy; the servant could not hold Him and had to lower Him to the earth. Returning, Jagadisha understood: Jagannatha wished to remain here. The Lord Himself becomes light when He wishes to be carried, and heavy when He chooses His place.

There is a tradition that Jagadisha brought the Deity from Puri on a pole; this pole — “the staff of Jagadisha Pandita” — is kept to this day in the temple of Jagannatha and shown to pilgrims.

Chakdaha is an ancient holy place. In the age of the Puranas its name was Rathavarma; at the end of the Dvapara-yuga Pradyumna, Krishna's son, slew the demon Shambara here, and the place came to be called Pradyumna-nagara; and when Bhagiratha led the Ganga to deliver the descendants of Sagara, the wheel (chakra) of his chariot sank here — hence the name “Chakradaha,” now Chakdah.11

The news that Jagannatha had come from Purushottama to Yashada spread far, and countless people began to flock to Him. Since Jagannatha had remained in Yashada, Jagadisha decided to live there and never returned to Mayapur. According to one of the biographies, Jagadisha and Hiranya moved from Mayapur “probably” after the Lord's sannyasa.

The Shripat at Yashada

At first Jagannatha stood under a banyan on the bank of the Ganga. Then Raja Krishnachandra of Goari-Krishnanagara helped to build a temple, and when it fell into disrepair it was restored by Mokshada Dasi, the wife of Umeshachandra Majumdar; according to the “Anubhashya,” this was in the year 1324 of the Bengali era, as an inscription on a stone slab records.

The temple has no dome (chura) and looks like an ordinary house. In it are Jagannathadeva, Radha-vallabha and Gaura-Gopala. Jagannatha's Snana-yatra is celebrated here every year with special splendour: a platform is set up on a wide field, and on the day of the Snana-yatra Jagannatha proceeds to it from the temple; the fair on this field is famous to this day. There is no Ratha-yatra here, according to one of the biographies. An old, crumbling dola-mancha, five centuries old, also survives: on Dola-purnima Radha-vallabha is brought out onto it.

The shripat stands in the village of Yashada (Yashora, Jashra) in the Nadia district, within a mile of Chakdaha station. In Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's time the Ganga had receded almost a krosha from it; the servitors were Vijayachandra Goswami and then Lalitamohana Goswami, of the Bandyopadhyaya line, and in Yashada they sang the suchaka-gana, a song of Jagadisha's life composed by the poet Gadadhara. For some time the siddha Bhagavan Dasa Babaji of Kalna lived and performed bhajana in Yashada; after settling in Kalna he would still come here from there.

The devotees donated much land to Jagannatha, but, according to one of the biographies, in time Jagadisha's descendants sold it to maintain the service. Later, when they could no longer carry it on, the temple passed to Srila Bhakti Dayita Madhava Maharaja, and since 1962 the shripat at Jashra has been one of the centres of the Sri Chaitanya Gaudiya Math. The biographers see a familiar pattern in this: just as the Gopala of Madhavendra Puri, so the Jagannatha and Gaura-Gopala of Jagadisha seemed Themselves to “offer Themselves” to Bhakti Dayita Madhava Maharaja — the Lord finds various ways to accept the service of the one He Himself has chosen.

Gaura-Gopala

Attracted by the parental love of Jagadisha and his wife, the Lord and Nityananda came to Yashada twice, held sankirtana there and celebrated a festival.12

When the Lord was ready to set out from Yashada for Nilachala, Dukhini wept in separation from Him. To console her, the Lord agreed to remain in Yashada in the form of the Deity — Gaura-Gopala. According to one of the biographies, this was after a festival of many days in Jagadisha's house, and Gaurasundara said to her: “I shall live for ever in your house in the form of the Deity.” Since then He has been served. Gaura-Gopala is golden in colour; according to the “Anubhashya,” He is a wooden Gopala, and Dukhini-mata herself installed Him. Gaura-Gopala is not a memorial image or a likeness: He is the Lord Himself, who remained in Yashada out of love for His devotee.

With Nityananda's Companions

Jagadisha was among Nityananda's companions at the chida-dadhi festival in Panihati:

“Dhananjaya, Jagadisha, Paramesvara dasa, Mahesha, Gauridasa, Krishnadasa Hoda.” (CC, Antya 6.62)

Together with the Gauda devotees he went to the Lord in Nilachala. Vrindavana Dasa writes how he and Hiranya set out together with Advaita:

“Sri Jagadisha Pandita and Hiranya Bhagavata also came joyfully, both intoxicated with the sweetness of the rasas of divine love for Krishna.” (CB, Antya 8.28)

Murari Gupta says the same (4.17.10); according to one of the biographies, Jagadisha went with the Gaudiyas to the Ratha-yatra every year.

Probably it was he who was among the devotees when, after His sannyasa, the Lord met Shachi in Shantipura: Vrindavana Dasa names in the list Haridasa, Murari, Shrigarbha, Narayana, Jagadisha and Gopinatha (CB, Antya 4.273). And when at the festival in Kheturi the Lord appeared with His associates, the “Bhakti-ratnakara” names Jagadisha too among the dancers (10.551; so also the “Narottama-vilasa” 7.110).

His dearest disciple was Raghunatha, or Raghunathacharya, the son of the lame Bhagavan; the “Narottama-vilasa” tells how he met Jahnava-devi on her journey (6.214–215), and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls him a disciple of Jagadisha Pandita Goswami.

Appearance and Disappearance

In our calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math the appearance day of Srila Jagadisha Pandita is Gaura Ekadashi of the month of Narayana (in 2027, 18 January),13 and his disappearance day is Gaura Tritiya of the same month (in 2027, 10 January). The biographies and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta also name the shukla-tritiya of the month of Pausha as the day of his departure; on this day a festival is held every year in Yashada. The sources do not give the year of his appearance or departure, nor do they say plainly where he left this world.14

Significance

Jagadisha Pandita is Chandrahasa, the dancer of Vraja, and one of the priests' wives who fed Krishna; in Gaura's pastimes he is a branch of both Chaitanya and Nityananda, the one who, in Krishnadasa Kaviraja's words, purifies the whole world and pours down the nectar of love for Krishna like a monsoon rain.

In his life the Lord revealed two sides of His love for His devotees. As an infant He Himself demanded his offering on Ekadashi, showing that fasting is the service of the servants, while the Lord accepts what is prepared for Him with love and joyfully eats what belongs to His devotee. And Jagannatha, seeing his longing in separation, Himself wished to go with him from Purushottama, Himself became light and Himself chose His place; and Gaura, moved by Dukhini's tears, Himself remained in her house as Gaura-Gopala. Parental love such as Jagadisha and Dukhini had for the Lord is accessible only to His eternal associates, and the Lord finds ways to accept the service of those whom He Himself has chosen.

Notes

  1. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Jagadisha, the son of Advaita Acharya, who turned away from Gaura; Jagadishvara, a disciple of Shyamananda; Jagadisha Raya of the “Narottama-vilasa”; Jagadisha Bhakti Pradipa (later Bhakti Pradipa Tirtha Maharaja); and Lala Jagadish Prasad. “Sri Jagadisha” in Murari Gupta (4.20.5) and in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (13) is Jagannatha Himself. Hiranya Pandita, Jagadisha's neighbour in Navadvipa, is not Hiranya Majumdar of Saptagrama.
  2. One of the biographies writes that “according to the Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” some consider Jagadisha and Hiranya to be naga-patni, the wives of the serpent Kaliya, and others that Jagadisha was the dancer Chandrahasa. In the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” (192) they are the priests' wives; there is nothing there about naga-patni in their regard.
  3. One of the biographies calls Kamalaksha “the son of Bhatta Narayana”; according to the “Anubhashya,” he only came of the line of Bhatta-narayana, the ancient progenitor of the Bengali brahmanas.
  4. Two biographies say that Hiranya came with Jagadisha to the Ganga; the third, like the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 11.30, says his younger brother Mahesha Pandita. In Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's account of the Yashada shripat tradition the brother is called simply Mahesha, without “Pandita.” According to the opinion of “some,” which the biographies give in their chapters on Mahesha Pandita, there were three brothers — Jagadisha, Hiranya and Mahesha Pandita; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, citing this opinion in the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 11.32, doubts only whether this Mahesha is the gopala Mahesha Pandita: the authoritative books do not say so. Jayananda in his “Chaitanya-mangala” calls Jagadisha and Hiranya brothers by birth, very dear to Nityananda, living in Navadvipa. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and the “Charitamrita” do not name any kinship: for them it is “two brahmanas,” “Jagadisha and Hiranya.”
  5. One of the biographies in one place refers to these verses as “CB 1.9.98–99” — a misprint: elsewhere in the same book it is correctly “1.2.98–99.” The biographies and the “Anubhashya” (following the shripat tradition) name Gauhati as Jagadisha's birthplace; the verse of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” says only that these associates lived hidden in Nadia, while in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” on CB, Adi 2.31, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta names Hiranya and Jagadisha among the devotees born in Navadvipa.
  6. We follow the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”: it was the brahmanas themselves who wondered and themselves brought the food, and it was Shachi who voiced the doubt. The biographies in their chapter on Jagadisha tell it otherwise: Jagannatha Mishra wondered, went himself to Jagadisha, saw the lavish preparations, told him of his son's request and of his fear that eating Vishnu's offering (rice) on Ekadashi did not befit the child, and Jagadisha at once gave him the whole offering; in the chapter on Mishra, that Mishra went to both friends. According to the “Charitamrita” (Adi 14.39), the Lord pretended to be ill; Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” that He said He would get well if He ate Vishnu's offering and sent His father there; the brahmanas wondered how so small a child could know of the offering and sent the food, and He fed the other children with it and ate a little Himself. According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.1111–1113), the food was brought even before it had been offered to Vishnu. Jayananda in his “Chaitanya-mangala” only briefly recalls: “Day and night Jagadisha in the house of Hiranya — on the day of Hari the Lord ate their offering.”
  7. In the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Adi 6.19–33) there is neither the vision of the infant Krishna, nor the jest, nor Nimai's coming to their house Himself: the brahmanas only understood that Gopala Himself was acting in the child's body; nor are there the words “Vishnu is not bound by the fast.” This is the biography's retelling.
  8. The biographies and the “Anubhashya” refer to the fourth chapter of the Adi-khanda — by the old numbering of the chapters.
  9. One of the biographies gives the reference “CB, Madhya 13.150” for the procession; that verse concerns Jagai and Madhai, while the procession on the day of the Kazi is Madhya 23.150. It refers the sport in the Ganga to Madhya 13.337; in our numbering the list occupies verses 336–339.
  10. According to one of the biographies, the Lord sent him to Nilachala even before His sannyasa; another holds that he moved to Yashada “probably” after the sannyasa. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta and the third biography give no time.
  11. The biographies differ in the order: one tells of Bhagiratha after Pradyumna, another “before that.”
  12. So also the “Anubhashya”: “it is said, twice.” One of the biographies writes “from time to time.”
  13. The biographies and the “Anubhashya” name the shukla-dvadashi of the month of Pausha as his appearance day.
  14. One of the biographies names as the day of his departure the thirteenth day after the full moon of Pausha (krishna-trayodashi); in our calendar this is the disappearance day of Mahesha Pandita — apparently the two festivals have been confused.
